claim: Biologically-controlled mineralization producing organic-inorganic composites (hard skeletons) by metazoan biomineralizers has been an evolutionary innovation since the earliest Cambrian.
source: Biologically-controlled mineralization producing organic-inorganic composites (hard skeletons) by metazoan biomineralizers has been an evolutionary innovation since the earliest Cambrian.
evidence: This is a general statement about the timing of biomineralization evolution, presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Linguliform brachiopods are one of the key invertebrates that secrete calcium phosphate minerals to build their shells.
source: Among them, linguliform brachiopods are one of the key invertebrates that secrete calcium phosphate minerals to build their shells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about linguliform brachiopods' biomineralization.

claim: The organo-phosphatic cylindrical column is exclusive to phosphatic-shelled brachiopods, including both crown and stem groups.
source: One of the most distinct shell structures is the organo-phosphatic cylindrical column exclusive to phosphatic-shelled brachiopods, including both crown and stem groups.
evidence: This is a statement about the distribution of columnar structures, presented as established knowledge.

claim: Exquisitely well-preserved columnar shell ultrastructures are reported for the first time in the earliest eoobolids Latusobolus xiaoyangbaensis gen. et sp. nov. and Eoobolus acutulus sp. nov. from the Cambrian Series 2 Shuijingtuo Formation of South China.
source: Here, exquisitely well-preserved columnar shell ultrastructures are reported for the first time in the earliest eoobolids Latusobolus xiaoyangbaensis gen. et sp. nov. and Eoobolus acutulus sp. nov. from the Cambrian Series 2 Shuijingtuo Formation of South China.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the specimens and analyses presented.

claim: The calcium phosphate-based biomineralized shells of Latusobolus xiaoyangbaensis and Eoobolus acutulus are mainly composed of stacked sandwich columnar units.
source: Their calcium phosphate-based biomineralized shells are mainly composed of stacked sandwich columnar units.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the specimens described in the study.

claim: The secretion and construction of the stacked sandwich model of columnar architecture is highly biologically controlled and organic-matrix mediated.
source: The secretion and construction of the stacked sandwich model of columnar architecture, which played a significant role in the evolution of linguliforms, is highly biologically controlled and organic-matrix mediated.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed structures and comparison with known biomineralization processes.

claim: A continuous transformation of anatomic features resulting from the growth of diverse columnar shells is revealed between Eoobolidae, Lingulellotretidae, and Acrotretida.
source: Furthermore, a continuous transformation of anatomic features resulting from the growth of diverse columnar shells is revealed between Eoobolidae, Lingulellotretidae, and Acrotretida, shedding new light on the evolutionary growth and adaptive innovation of biomineralized columnar architecture among early phosphatic-shelled brachiopods during the Cambrian explosion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparative analysis of shell structures across different taxa.

claim: The early Cambrian witnessed a great burst in diversity of animal body plans and biomineralized shell architectures around half a billion years ago.
source: The early Cambrian witnessed a great burst in diversity of animal body plans and biomineralized shell architectures around half a billion years ago (Briggs, 2015; Erwin, 2015; Erwin, 2020; Budd and Jackson, 2016; Murdock, 2020; Yun et al., 2021; Zhang and Shu, 2021; Zhang et al., 2021c).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Biologically-controlled mineralization played a vital role in the survival and fitness of early clades.
source: The novel process of biologically-controlled mineralization producing organic-inorganic composites (hard skeletons) in complex animals had played a vital role in the survival and fitness of early clades (Balthasar, 2009; Cuif et al., 2010; Li et al., 2022; Skovsted et al., 2008; Yun et al., 2022)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Biomineralization built the fundamental blocks of complex marine ecosystems.
source: and in turn built the fundamental blocks of complex marine ecosystems (Bicknell and Paterson, 2018; Buatois et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Phosphatic-shelled brachiopods are some of the most common animals in early Cambrian faunas.
source: Among them, the phosphatic-shelled brachiopods are some of the most common animals in early Cambrian faunas (Harper et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Brachiopods are unique animals in having the ability to secrete two different minerals, calcium phosphate and calcium carbonate.
source: Brachiopods are unique animals in having the ability to secrete two different minerals, calcium phosphate and calcium carbonate, making them the ideal group to further explore the processes of biomineralization (Simonet Roda et al., 2022; Williams, 1997a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Hard tissues composed of calcium phosphate with an organic matrix are largely present in vertebrates.
source: Hard tissues composed of calcium phosphate with an organic matrix are also largely present in vertebrates, which have remarkably shaped the evolutionary trajectory of life on Earth (Ruben and Bennett, 1987; Wood and Zhuravlev, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The origin of phosphate biomineralization in the evolutionary distant invertebrate brachiopods and vertebrates is still a big mystery in animal evolution.
source: The origin of phosphate biomineralization in the evolutionary distant invertebrate brachiopods and vertebrates is still a big mystery in animal evolution (Luo et al., 2015; Neary et al., 2011; Roda and Mar, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations indicating this is an open question in the field.

claim: South China has been considered as one of centres for the origination and early dispersal of phosphatic-shelled brachiopods.
source: It is noteworthy that South China has been considered as one of centres for the origination and early dispersal of phosphatic-shelled brachiopods (Zhang et al., 2021a)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The shell-forming process of brachiopods has long been problematic.
source: The shell-forming process of brachiopods, although critical to understanding their poorly resolved phylogeny and early evolution, has long been problematic (Carlson, 2016; Cusack and Williams, 2007; Holmer et al., 2008a; Murdock, 2020; Streng et al., 2007; Temereva, 2022; Williams et al., 2004; Williams and Cusack, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The epithelial cells of the outer mantle lobes have been considered to be responsible for the shell ornamentation and fabrics of brachiopods.
source: The epithelial cells of the outer mantle lobes have been considered to be responsible for the shell ornamentation and fabrics of brachiopods (Williams and Cusack, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The biologically controlled process of brachiopod shell secretion at the cellular level is still unclear.
source: However, the biologically controlled process of brachiopod shell secretion at the cellular level is still unclear, although organic substrates are observed to be available for biomineral deposition during mantle activity (Williams et al., 1997b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation indicating this is an open question in the field.

claim: Most studies on brachiopod shells are focused on articulated or carbonate-shelled representatives.
source: Extensive studies have been conducted on living and fossil shells, but most of them are focused on articulated or carbonate-shelled representatives (Cusack et al., 2010; Griesshaber et al., 2007; Simonet Roda et al., 2022; Roda and Mar, 2021; Ye et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The building of shells by microscopic cylindrical columns is a unique feature restricted to the phosphatic-shelled brachiopods and their assumed ancestors.
source: The building of shells by microscopic cylindrical columns is a unique feature, which is restricted to the phosphatic-shelled brachiopods and their assumed ancestors (Butler et al., 2015; Holmer et al., 2002; Holmer et al., 2008b; Holmer, 1989; Skovsted and Holmer, 2003; Williams and Holmer, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Columnar shell was previously believed to be exclusively restricted to micromorphic acrotretide brachiopods.
source: This type of columnar shell was previously believed to be exclusively restricted to micromorphic acrotretide brachiopods, a group that demonstrates more complex hierarchical architectures and graded structures compared to simple lamella shell structure in older lingulides (Holmer, 1989; Williams and Holmer, 1992).

claim: Diverse columnar shell architectures occur in other brachiopod groups, including stem group taxa, such as Mickwitzia, Setatella, and Micrina.
source: Further studies, however, reveal that diverse columnar shell architectures occur in other brachiopod groups, including stem group taxa, such as Mickwitzia, Setatella, and Micrina (Butler et al., 2015; Holmer et al., 2008a; Skovsted et al., 2010; Skovsted and Holmer, 2003; Williams and Holmer, 2002)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Columnar architectures occur in the lingulellotretid Lingulellotreta.
source: the lingulellotretid Lingulellotreta (Holmer et al., 2008b)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Columnar architectures occur in the eoobolid Eoobolus.
source: the eoobolid Eoobolus (Zhang et al., 2021a)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Columnar architectures occur in the enigmatic Bistramia.
source: and the enigmatic Bistramia (Holmer et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The columnar architectures among the oldest linguliforms and their evolutionary variations have not been studied in detail.
source: However, the columnar architectures among the oldest linguliforms and their evolutionary variations have not been studied in detail.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Different conditions of fossil preservation with varied taphonomic histories often obscure the finer details of shell structures.
source: Different conditions of fossil preservation with varied taphonomic histories have compounded this issue as different depositional environments, pore-water geochemistry, and subsequent diagenetic and tectonic alteration often obscure the finer details of shell structures (Butler et al., 2015; Holmer et al., 2008a; Streng et al., 2007; Ushatinskaya and Korovnikov, 2014; Zhang, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Holmer et al., 1996 established the Eoobolidae to include lingulides characterized by a pitted metamorphic shell and a post-metamorphic shell with pustules.
source: Holmer et al., 1996 established the Eoobolidae to include lingulides characterized by a pitted metamorphic shell and a post-metamorphic shell with pustules.

source: The shell architectures are exquisitely well-preserved in these newly assigned eoobolid Latusobolus xiaoyangbaensis gen. et sp. nov. and Eoobolus acutulus sp. nov.

source: The hollow space in the columns and between lamellae of stacked columnar units may be originally filled with the rich composition of organic material (Figures 1C, I, 2C, F, H and Figure 3E; Appendix 1—figure 4I).

source: Columns are quite small about 2.4 μm in diameter, ranging from 1.6 μm to 3.4 μm, and about 6 μm in height, ranging from 2.9 μm to 11.9 μm.

claim: The supposed living fossil Lingula has long been considered to virtually lack morphological evolutionary changes.
source: Although the supposed living fossil Lingula has long been considered to virtually lack morphological evolutionary changes (Schopf, 1984)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Lingulide brachiopods have experienced dramatic modifications in many aspects.
source: more recent studies have shown that lingulide brachiopods have experienced dramatic modifications in many aspects (Liang et al., 2023), including arrangement of internal organs (Zhang et al., 2008), life mode (Topper et al., 2015), shell structure (Cusack et al., 1999), and even genome (Goto et al., 2022; Luo et al., 2015).

source: The complexity and diversity of linguliform shell architecture was increasingly recognised in the pioneering study of Cusack, Williams and Holmer (Cusack et al., 1999; Holmer, 1989; Williams and Cusack, 1999; Williams and Holmer, 1992).

claim: Complex architectures had a wide distribution in closely related brachiopod groups when they made their first appearance at the beginning of the Cambrian.

source: However, compared to their ancestral representatives, the shell structure in living lingulides is relatively simple, revealing profound modifications during their long evolutionary history (Cusack et al., 1999; Holmer et al., 2008a; Williams, 1997a; Williams and Cusack, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The shells of organo-phosphatic brachiopods are stratiform, composed of an outer periostracum and inner rhythmically-disposed succession of biomineralized lamellae or laminae.
source: In general, the shells of organo-phosphatic brachiopods are stratiform, composed of an outer periostracum and inner rhythmically-disposed succession of biomineralized lamellae or laminae (Holmer, 1989; Williams et al., 1997b).

claim: The organic periostracum is rarely fossilized.
source: The organic periostracum, serving as a rheological coat to the underlying shell, is rarely fossilized.

claim: The wrinkling and vesicular features of the periostracum have largely been preserved as superficial imprints on the surface of the primary layer.
source: However, its wrinkling and vesicular features have largely been preserved as superficial imprints (pits, pustules, fila, grooves, ridges, rugellae, drapes, reticulate networks, and spines) on the surface of the primary layer (Figure 3A and B)

claim: Superficial imprints on the primary layer are important characters in understanding brachiopod phylogeny.
source: and are important characters in understanding brachiopod phylogeny (Holmer, 1989; Holmer et al., 1996; Cusack et al., 1999).

source: By contrast, the structures preserved in the secondary layer have been characterised in fossil and living groups by three ancient fabrics –columnar, baculate, laminated – all of which persist in living shells except for the columnar fabric (Cusack et al., 1999).

claim: The tertiary shell layer is well developed in some recent and Palaeozoic lingulides.

source: Although different in size, the similar pattern may indicate the same secretion regime that originated as vesicles during the very early stages of periostracum secretion (Cusack et al., 1999).

claim: The fossil record reveals that the columnar shell structure is generally preserved in most early linguliforms.
source: The fossil record reveals that the columnar shell structure (Figure 3G–I and Figure 4) is generally preserved in most early linguliforms (Holmer et al., 2008b; Streng et al., 2007; Williams et al., 1997b; Zhang, 2018; Zhang et al., 2021a).
